As of December 31, 2023, Boeing’s filing reported:

- **21%** — International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (**IAM**)
- **10%** — Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (**SPEEA**)
- **1%** — United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (**UAW**)

The filing also said about **57,000 employees** were union members. These listed percentages total **32%**; the filing separately states in a risk-factor discussion that unions represented **33%** of the workforce. Source: Boeing 2023 Form 10-K, Human Capital (p. 5) and Supply Chain and Labor Risks (p. 12).

The filing dates these developments in **calendar 2025**:

- **April 23 — EU Digital Markets Act investigations:** The European Commission fined Apple **€500 million** and ordered it to remove certain restrictions on developers steering users to alternative offers outside the App Store. Apple appealed. The Commission also issued **preliminary findings** in a separate DMA investigation concerning Apple’s contractual requirements for app developers and marketplaces.
- **April 30 — Epic Games litigation:** A California federal court found Apple had violated the 2021 injunction, barred Apple from imposing fees on certain out-of-app purchases or restricting how developers direct customers to them, denied Apple’s request to narrow or vacate the injunction, and referred the matter to the U.S. Attorney to consider criminal-contempt proceedings. Apple appealed.
- **September 2 — Google antitrust matter:** A federal district court ordered remedies after finding Google had violated U.S. antitrust laws. The filing says the order remained subject to further proceedings and appeals, with potential consequences for Apple’s search-licensing arrangements with Google.
- **October — Epic Games appeal:** The Ninth Circuit heard oral arguments on an expedited basis in Apple’s appeal.

*Source: Apple’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A (p. 17) and Item 3 (p. 21).*

Apple’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K reports these percentages:

| Percentage | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **40%** | Fiscal 2025 net sales through Apple’s **direct** distribution channels. |
| **60%** | Fiscal 2025 net sales through Apple’s **indirect** distribution channels. |
| **12%** | **Total trade receivables** as of September 27, 2025, attributable to one customer. |
| **34%** | **Total trade receivables** as of September 27, 2025, attributable to third-party cellular network carriers. |
| **46%** and **23%** | **Total vendor non-trade receivables** as of September 27, 2025, attributable to each of two manufacturing vendors. |

The channel figures are on page 5; the receivables figures are on page 42. The filing says the vendor receivables arise from component sales to manufacturing vendors; those sales are not included in product net sales.

The filing gives these related but distinct figures:

- **Strike:** IAM District 837 represented **approximately 3,200 Boeing employees at St. Louis-area sites**—the represented workforce, not a separately stated count of employees who actually struck. The work stoppage began **August 4, 2025** and ended when employees voted to ratify a new contract on **November 13, 2025**; Boeing describes it as lasting **101 days**. It disrupted St. Louis operations and affected programs including F/A-18, F-15, T-7A, MQ-25 and Weapons.
- **Current agreement:** Boeing’s collective-bargaining-agreement table lists **IAM District 837, Missouri**, with an expiration date of **July 2030**. That is the listed end date for the agreement, not the strike’s duration.

The strike details appear on Form 10-K pages 4, 11 and 26; the agreement expiration appears on page 4.

Boeing’s 2025 Form 10-K gives these shares:

- **46%** of Boeing’s **total 2025 revenue** came from non-U.S. customers, including Foreign Military Sales through the U.S. government.
- **60%** of **Commercial Airplanes revenue from customer contracts** came from non-U.S. customers.
- **Approximately 85%** of **Commercial Airplanes’ total backlog, measured in dollars**, was with non-U.S. airlines.
- **26%** of **Defense, Space & Security backlog** was attributable to non-U.S. customers as of December 31, 2025.

The revenue figures are stated on page 12; the backlog figures on pages 35 and 40.

Apple said foreign-currency weakness against the U.S. dollar was a headwind to:

- **Net sales in Greater China**—specifically, weakness in the **renminbi** had an unfavorable year-over-year impact.
- **Net sales in Japan**—weakness in the **yen** had an unfavorable impact, even though Japan sales increased overall.
- **Net sales in Rest of Asia Pacific**—foreign-currency weakness had a net unfavorable impact, although sales in the segment also increased.
- **Products gross margin and Products gross-margin percentage**—currency weakness partly offset the increases in both measures.

These comparisons are for fiscal 2024 versus fiscal 2023. (Form 10-K, MD&A, pp. 22–24.)

For 2022, Boeing’s filing says revenue recognized on fixed-price contracts was:

- **Commercial Airplanes (BCA): 100%**
- **Defense, Space & Security (BDS): 60%**
- **Global Services (BGS): 88%**

The percentages are reported in Note 22’s segment revenue tables.

The filing gives these dividend-related dollar amounts for the 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock:

| Amount | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **Up to $345 million per year** | Boeing’s estimate of the **annual cash it might need** for preferred dividends through the October 15, 2027 mandatory conversion date. This is a projected cash requirement, not a dividend declared or paid. (p. 17) |
| **$72 million** | Dividends **declared in December 2024** for holders of record January 1, 2025, and **paid in cash on January 15, 2025**. (p. 106; also shown as cash dividends declared in the equity statement, p. 58) |
| **$12.50 per preferred share** | The per-share amount represented by that **$72 million declaration**. (p. 106) |
| **$58 million** | Dividends **accumulated during 2024** for the financial statements’ earnings-per-share calculation. Boeing subtracts this from net loss attributable to Boeing shareholders to arrive at net loss attributable to common shareholders. It is an accounting-period amount, distinct from the $72 million declared. (pp. 54, 59, 73) |

The filing describes these effects as having occurred or possibly having occurred:

- **Blocked shipments and support:** Sanctions and export controls imposed in response to the war blocked NVIDIA products, services, and support from going into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine.
- **Russia operations stopped:** In fiscal 2023, NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia and later closed its business operations there. The filing says direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2022 had been immaterial.
- **Sales in EMEA were affected:** The war impacted end-customer sales in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (EMEA).
- **Sales through partners may have been affected:** NVIDIA said revenue from partners selling into Russia *may have been negatively impacted* by the war.

These statements appear in the filing’s regulatory-risk discussion and fiscal 2023 management discussion (pp. 28, 37). I have excluded effects described only as possible future consequences.

For fiscal 2024, NVIDIA disclosed:

- **$774 million** in inventory provisions charged to cost of revenue, for inventory write-downs.
- **Approximately $1.4 billion** in cost of revenue for inventory purchase obligations above current demand projections, supplier charges, and penalties related to cancellations and underutilization.
- **$540 million in provision releases**, resulting from sales of previously reserved inventory **or** settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations. The filing does not split the release between those two sources.

Together, the two charges amount to approximately **$2.174 billion**; NVIDIA describes provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations as **$2.2 billion**. (Form 10-K, pp. 40, 68, 70.)

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2026 Form 10-K gives these goodwill amounts, in U.S. dollars:

- **$20.8 billion total balance at January 25, 2026**: **$20.5 billion** was allocated to the Compute & Networking reporting unit and **$370 million** to Graphics. The segment figures are rounded.
- **$15.6 billion added during fiscal 2026**: allocated to Compute & Networking.
- **$14.4 billion recorded for the Groq technology license**: primarily represented the workforce and future development of the licensed technology; it was assigned to Compute & Networking and was tax deductible. This is a specific goodwill addition disclosed in the year, not a separate year-end balance.

The filing says its annual qualitative impairment tests found no goodwill impairment. (Form 10-K, Notes 2 and 5, pp. 61 and 63.)

For fiscal 2025, the filing reports these investment-related amounts, in millions:

- **Publicly-held equity securities:** **$88 realized gains** on securities sold. This is the difference between sale proceeds and the securities’ carrying value at the beginning of the period—or their purchase date, if later.
- **Non-marketable equity securities:** **$816 in unrealized gains** and **$59 in impairments and unrealized losses**, a **net gain of $757** in those reported adjustments. The filing says a fourth-quarter secondary transaction in one private-company investment produced an **unrealized gain of $565**, included in the $816.

The filing says gains and losses on non-marketable investments, realized and unrealized, are recognized in **Other income (expense), net**. I have excluded the **$163** of unrealized gains on publicly-held securities still held at year-end, cumulative gains and losses on non-marketable securities still held, fiscal 2024 amounts, and the total for Other, net. (Form 10-K, pp. 43, 66, 68–69.)

The filing reports these PTC-specific amounts **as of December 31, 2023**:

| Amount | What it represents |
|---:|---|
| **$21.404 billion** | PTC identifiable assets at year-end, in the business-segment table. |
| **$6.605 billion** | PTC goodwill at year-end, shown separately in that table. |
| **Approximately $6.6 billion** | PTC-related net intangible assets included in the consolidated railroad, utilities and energy balance. |
| **Approximately $2.1 billion** | PTC-related receivables included in consolidated railroad, utilities and energy receivables. |
| **Approximately $1.7 billion** | PTC-attributable inventories, materials and supplies included in consolidated other assets. |
| **$5.776 billion** | PTC and subsidiaries’ notes payable and other borrowings. |

Sources: Note 8, K-88; Notes 9, 10 and 13, K-89–K-91; Note 19, K-102; and Note 26, K-114. The identifiable-assets, goodwill and intangible-asset figures are separate disclosures but not all independent amounts to sum; the intangible assets are part of the broader asset balances. I’ve excluded year flows and acquisition-date figures.

The filing gives these figures for Upjohn separation costs:

- **“approximately $700 million”** — Pfizer’s expected total costs in connection with separating Upjohn.
- **“approximately 75%”** — the portion Pfizer said had been incurred from inception through December 31, 2021.
- **“$434 million in 2020 and $83 million in 2019”** — separation-related costs actually incurred in those years and included in discontinued operations. Pfizer said these primarily related to professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities in finance, tax, legal and information systems, as well as investment-banking fees.

The filing also says the expected costs included expenses related to **“separation of legal entities and transaction costs.”** (MD&A, p. 26; Note 2B, p. 65.)

As of **January 31, 2022**, the filing gives these counts:

- **Walmart U.S.:** “approximately **4,600 pickup locations**” and “more than **3,500 same-day delivery locations**.” These are Walmart U.S. omnichannel services. (Form 10-K, p. 7)
- **Walmart International:** “approximately **2,900 pickup** and **over 1,900 delivery locations**.” These are Walmart International’s pickup and delivery services. (p. 9)

The filing describes the U.S. delivery figure specifically as **same-day**; it does not attach that qualifier to the International delivery figure. These are customer-service locations, not distribution or fulfillment facility counts.

JPMorgan Chase’s 2023 Form 10-K reports these effects from adopting the TDR guidance on January 1, 2023 (all amounts in **millions of dollars**):

| Amount | What it measures |
|---:|---|
| **$587 decrease** | The Firm’s net reduction in the **allowance for credit losses**. The Form 10-K’s allowance rollforward identifies this as the cumulative adoption effect on the **allowance for loan losses**. |
| **$489 decrease** | Adoption effect on the allowance for loan losses for **Consumer, excluding credit card**. |
| **$100 decrease** | Adoption effect on the allowance for loan losses for **Credit card**. |
| **$2 increase** | Adoption effect on the allowance for loan losses for **Wholesale**. |
| **$446 increase** | Increase in **retained earnings, after tax**, from the modified-retrospective adoption. |

The portfolio figures net to the **$587 million decrease**. The Form 10-K says the retained-earnings increase was predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card. Sources: Note 1, Form 10-K p. 173; allowance tables, pp. 132 and 258.

The filing identifies **two operating businesses** with 2024 affiliate-borrowing amounts:

| Business | Affiliate borrowing amount disclosed for 2024 |
|---|---|
| **Clayton Homes** | Borrowings from Berkshire finance affiliates **increased $6.6 billion**, reaching **$24.3 billion** at December 31, 2024. |
| **Pilot Travel Centers** | Borrowed **$5.7 billion** from Berkshire insurance subsidiaries in March, then repaid **$1.0 billion** during 2024. Those disclosed transactions imply **$4.7 billion** remained from the advances, though the filing doesn’t state that as a separate year-end balance. |

Sources: Form 10-K pages **K-48** (Clayton) and **K-53** (Pilot). The borrowing amounts above exclude interest.

Pfizer’s 2024 Form 10-K gives these Haleon ownership percentages:

- **32% as of December 31, 2023.**
- **Approximately 23% after the March 2024 share sale.**
- **Approximately 15% after the October 2024 sale, and as of December 31, 2024.**

The filing discusses the sales and ownership changes in Note 3, “Equity-Method Investments” (Form 10-K p. 75).

Walmart’s fiscal 2025 filing reports these long-term debt repayments, in millions of U.S. dollars:

- **$3,468** — “Repayments of long-term debt” in the fiscal 2025 cash-flow statement; the same total appears in the long-term debt balance rollforward. (pp. 44, 57)
- **$3,373** — “Total repayment of matured debt” for the significant fiscal 2025 maturities itemized in Note 6:
  - **$1,500** — matured April 22, 2024
  - **$990** — matured July 8, 2024
  - **$253** — repayment on ¥40,000 of debt, matured July 18, 2024
  - **$630** — matured December 15, 2024 (p. 69)

The $3,373 is the total for the specifically listed matured-debt repayments; the $3,468 is the broader repayment amount reported in the cash-flow statement and debt rollforward.

The 2025 Form 10-K lists Huizhou’s annual capacity as:

- **Ethylene: 1.6 million metric tons per year**
- **Polyethylene: 1.7 million metric tons per year**
- **Polypropylene: 0.9 million metric tons per year**

These are the complex’s capacity figures for each product, not an aggregate tonnage figure. The table reports Huizhou at **100% ExxonMobil interest**. (Form 10-K, p. 23; capacities shown in millions of metric tons per year.)

The Form 10-K identifies these fiscal 2024 results as benefiting from lapping fiscal 2023 items:

| Fiscal 2024 result | Item lapped |
|---|---|
| **Gross profit rate** increased 27 basis points on a consolidated basis; the filing says the increase was driven primarily by Walmart U.S. | Higher markdowns incurred in the prior year. The Walmart U.S. segment discussion separately reports a 20-basis-point increase and names higher net markdowns as the lapped item. |
| **Operating expenses as a percentage of net sales** decreased 60 basis points on a consolidated basis. | $3.3 billion in opioid-related legal-settlement charges and $0.8 billion in reorganization and restructuring charges in Walmart International, both from fiscal 2023. |
| **Walmart International operating expenses as a percentage of segment net sales** decreased 152 basis points. | Fiscal 2023 business reorganization and restructuring charges related to Flipkart and Massmart. |
| **Sam’s Club gross profit rate** increased 55 basis points. | Elevated markdowns in the prior year. |
| **Return on investment (ROI)** increased to 15.0% from 12.7%. | Opioid-related legal-settlement charges and reorganization and restructuring expenses, all recorded in fiscal 2023. |
| **Operating income as a percentage of net sales** increased 83 basis points. | The filing says this reflected the factors described above, which include lapping the markdowns and charges. |

The consolidated gross-profit discussion and its later consolidated-results discussion refer to the same result, so I’ve counted it once. The Walmart U.S. segment’s gross-profit rate is a separate segment result. (Form 10-K, pp. 38, 41–44.)

The 2021 Form 10-K names three projects as **funded during 2021** and two as reaching a **final investment decision (FID)**:

| Project | 2021 status |
|---|---|
| **Bacalhau Phase 1** development, Brazil | Funded; ExxonMobil also announced its FID in June 2021. |
| **North Field Production Sustainment Integrated Drilling and Looping**, Qatar | Funded. |
| **Jansz-Io Compression**, Australia | Funded. |
| **Multi-billion-dollar chemical complex in Huizhou, China** | FID reached. |

Bacalhau Phase 1 is the project appearing in both categories. The project-specific references are on the report’s printed pages 16–18 and 46–53.

The filing says the initial effects of COVID-19 were particularly severe for commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers. In reassessing PCC and certain other reporting units in the second quarter of 2020, Berkshire considered airlines’ announcements about expected future demand, employment levels and aircraft orders; manufacturers’ announcements of reduced aircraft production; and actions Berkshire was taking or might take to restructure operations. In light of those circumstances, Berkshire judged it prudent to raise discount rates and reduce its prior long-term forecasts of future cash flows. Those valuation changes led to the impairment charges, nearly all related to PCC.

As of January 31, 2026, the filing reports:

- **$6,020 million** — the swaps’ **notional amount**.
- **$920 million liability** — their **fair value**; the table shows it as **$(920) million**. In the market-risk discussion, Walmart describes this rounded as a **$0.9 billion liability**.

It also gives two **hypothetical sensitivities**, not additional balance-sheet amounts: a uniform 10% weakening of the U.S. dollar would change the swaps’ value by **$0.7 billion**, and a hypothetical 10% change in the underlying interest rates would change it by **$0.1 billion**. (Form 10-K, pp. 47, 69.)

Walmart’s fiscal 2022 Form 10-K gives these Flipkart-linked figures:

| Figure | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$3.2 billion** | Cash Walmart received during fiscal 2022, **primarily related to new equity funding for its majority-owned Flipkart subsidiary**. The funding reduced Walmart’s ownership from **approximately 83%** at January 31, 2021, to **approximately 75%**. |
| **Approximately $2.2 billion** | As of January 31, 2022, this portion of Walmart’s restricted cash could be accessed only through dividends or intercompany financing, subject to Flipkart minority-shareholder approval. Walmart said it expected the cash to be used by Flipkart. |
| **$0.4 billion** | Fiscal 2020 impairment charges in Walmart International, primarily the write-off of the carrying value of **Jabong.com**, one of Flipkart’s two fashion trade names, as Walmart focused on Myntra.com. |

Sources: Form 10-K pp. 42–43, 64 and 71. I’ve excluded broader segment or company totals that include Flipkart but aren’t specifically attributed to it.

Apple says quarter-to-quarter net sales can differ because of:

- **Seasonality:** Historically, first-quarter sales have been higher, partly because of holiday demand.
- **Product and service introductions:** Launches can significantly affect net sales.
- **Dependence on a major product:** A decline in demand for the product that accounts for a significant share of sales could materially affect quarterly sales.
- **Unexpected developments:** Lower-than-expected demand; problems with new product or service introductions; IT-system failures or network disruptions; or failures by logistics, component-supply, or manufacturing partners.

These are the filing’s sales-related factors, excluding its separate list of gross-margin volatility and downward-pressure factors. (Form 10-K, p. 18)

ExxonMobil gives these annual sensitivities:

| Change | Stated annual effect |
|---|---|
| **Brent crude: $1/barrel** | Approximately **$700 million after tax** on Upstream consolidated plus equity-company earnings |
| **Henry Hub gas: $0.10 per million Btu** | Approximately **$90 million after tax** on Upstream consolidated plus equity-company earnings |
| **TTF gas: $0.10 per million Btu** | Approximately **$20 million after tax** on Upstream consolidated plus equity-company earnings |
| **Long-term expected return on pension assets: 0.5 percentage-point decrease worldwide** | Approximately **$150 million higher annual pension expense before tax** |

The commodity sensitivities are for 2026 and **exclude derivatives**; ExxonMobil notes that actual results also depend on factors such as production, taxes, trading, and contract price lags. It also says a **100-basis-point interest-rate change affecting debt** would not be material to earnings or cash flow, but gives no dollar estimate for that change. (Form 10-K, MD&A “Market Risks,” p. 62; “Pension Benefits,” p. 67.)

The filing attributes PCC’s 11.6% revenue decline in 2021 to the continuing effects of COVID-19 on commercial aviation. Reduced air travel led aircraft manufacturers to cut production, while airlines delayed or cancelled orders and the industry reduced inventories. Those lower aircraft production levels weighed on PCC’s revenue in both 2020 and 2021.

More broadly, the sharp drop in air travel drove aircraft build-rate reductions and customer destocking “at extraordinary rates.” The filing also says production delays in Boeing’s 737 MAX and 787 programs adversely affected PCC over the preceding three years. (Form 10-K, pp. K-12 and K-49.)

The 2024 Form 10-K gives these figures for Pioneer’s scale and contribution:

- **Share of ExxonMobil at year-end 2024:** Pioneer represented **19% of consolidated assets** and **4% of consolidated revenues**. The report gives these percentages when explaining that Pioneer was excluded from the year-end internal-control assessment.
- **Pioneer’s actual 2024 contribution after the May 3 acquisition:** **$17.008 billion in sales and other operating revenues** and **$1.710 billion in net income attributable to ExxonMobil**, through December 31.
- **Proved reserves added through the acquisition:** **2.3 billion oil-equivalent barrels (GOEB)**, reported among the additions to proved reserves during 2024.

The report also says ExxonMobil’s **Permian** production averaged about **1,185 thousand oil-equivalent barrels per day** in 2024—about **570 thousand** above the prior year—but that is a basin-wide figure, not a separately stated Pioneer-only production contribution. (Form 10-K pp. 75, 121, 127; MD&A p. 49.)

The 10-K says consumer credit performance benefited from an improving macroeconomic environment. Lower card charge-offs reflected elevated consumer cash balances. Lower scored-auto charge-offs reflected higher vehicle collateral values and elevated consumer cash balances. In residential real estate, higher net recoveries reflected further home-price-index improvement and more reversals of prior write-downs from prepayments in the low-rate environment. (2021 Form 10-K, pp. 64, 111, 113–114)

The filing attributes the fiscal 2025 increases to:

- **Walmart overall:** Higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan, increased marketing, and higher depreciation expenses (p. 36).
- **Walmart U.S.:** Increased marketing, higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan, and increased depreciation expenses (p. 40).
- **Sam’s Club U.S.:** Higher compensation-related expenses—including associate wage investments and higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan—and elevated technology spending (p. 42).

Walmart International’s operating-expense ratio **decreased**, so it is not among the segments with an increase (p. 41).

The filing says these securities are investments in private companies with no readily determinable fair values. NVIDIA therefore uses the measurement alternative: it starts with cost, adjusts for impairment and observable transactions in similar investments of the same issuer, and may need unobservable valuation inputs. Those inputs include volatility, expected time to liquidity, the risk-free rate, and rights and obligations specific to each security. It also assesses impairment quarterly using judgment about factors such as the investee’s operating performance and market trends.
Higher average deposits associated with First Republic, transferred from Consumer & Community Banking to Asset & Wealth Management in the fourth quarter of 2023.

Pfizer said the increase in IPR&D gross carrying amount—from $3.092 billion to $11.357 billion—mainly reflected its acquisitions of Arena, GBT and Biohaven. Those acquisitions added approximately $5.0 billion, $3.0 billion and $450 million of IPR&D, respectively. The increase was partly offset by a $200 million impairment of an IPR&D asset acquired in the Array acquisition. Pfizer attributed that impairment to a Phase 3 trial reaching futility at a planned interim analysis for an unapproved symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy indication related to an LMNA gene mutation. (2022 Form 10-K, pp. 67, 74, 86.)

Pfizer attributes the **$1.052 billion favorable swing**—from $217 million of deductions in 2022 to $835 million of income in 2023—primarily to **net gains on equity securities in 2023 versus net losses in 2022**, and **lower net interest expense**. These benefits were **partly offset by much higher intangible-asset impairment charges** (Form 10-K, MD&A p. 40; Note 4, p. 73).

The equity-security result shifted from a **$1.273 billion net loss in 2022 to a $1.590 billion net gain in 2023**. Pfizer says 2023 included a **$1.7 billion realized gain on Telavant** and a **$297 million unrealized gain on Cerevel**, partly offset by a **$292 million unrealized loss on BioNTech**. The 2022 losses included **$986 million of unrealized losses** on investments in BioNTech, Allogene Therapeutics and Arvinas.

**Net interest expense fell by $402 million**, from $987 million to $585 million. Interest expense itself **increased by $971 million**, reflecting the **$31 billion of senior unsecured notes issued in May 2023 to help finance the Seagen acquisition**. But interest income **increased by $1.373 billion**, as Pfizer invested the net proceeds from that debt issuance; that more than offset the higher interest expense.

The offsetting impairment charges rose from **$421 million to $3.024 billion**. Pfizer says 2023’s charges were primarily intangible-asset impairments, including **$1.4 billion for etrasimod**, **$964 million for Prevnar 13** and **$486 million for other IPR&D and developed-technology assets**. The cited reasons included changed development plans and revenue expectations, updated commercial forecasts, competitive pressures and prioritization decisions.

Other year-over-year movements in Note 4 included favorable changes in **royalty-related income** ($845 million to $1.058 billion), **Haleon/Consumer Healthcare JV equity-method income** ($436 million to $505 million), and **“Other, net”** ($378 million to $1.002 billion). Pfizer says 2023 “Other, net” included ViiV and Nimbus dividend income and a **$222 million gain on the rare-disease gene-therapy portfolio divestiture**. Offsetting movements included **lower collaboration and out-licensing income** ($188 million to $154 million), **lower non-service benefit credits** ($849 million to $610 million), and **higher legal expenses** ($230 million to $474 million). (Note 4, p. 73.)

The filing attributes the fiscal 2026 gross profit rate increases to:

- **Company-wide (+8 basis points):** disciplined inventory management and growth in higher-margin businesses globally.
- **Walmart U.S. (+22 basis points):** disciplined inventory management and growth in higher-margin businesses.
- **Sam’s Club U.S. (+4 basis points):** operational efficiencies and higher fuel margins.

Walmart International’s gross profit rate decreased, so it is not included. (Form 10-K, pp. 35, 39, 41.)

The filing says the Permian and Guyana growth was more than offset by **divestments, the Russia expropriation, and lower production entitlements due to higher prices**. It also notes that easing government-mandated curtailments contributed to the overall production increase. (2022 Form 10-K, p. 52)

Credit-card net charge-offs rose with loan growth, including growth in new accounts and revolving balances. Wholesale net charge-offs rose primarily because of commercial-and-industrial losses, including in Technology, Media & Telecommunications and Healthcare, and estimated borrower-fraud losses in certain secured lending facilities. Asset & Wealth Management charge-offs increased largely because of a client-specific exposure charged off in the third quarter of 2025.

ExxonMobil attributes the sharp rise in 2022 refining margins to a **tight market**: gasoline and diesel demand had recovered to pre-pandemic levels, while pandemic-era refinery shutdowns and lack of investment had reduced industry capacity. It also cites low inventories and stronger trading and marketing margins as drivers of the improvement. Jet-fuel demand, by contrast, remained below historical levels because of continued COVID-19 impacts. (Form 10-K, pp. 47, 53–54)

Pfizer says the IPR&D gross carrying amount increased mainly because of about **$8.0 billion of IPR&D acquired with Metsera**. That was partly offset by **$3.9 billion of impairment charges** and transfers out of IPR&D to developed technology rights: **$600 million for Padcev** and **$590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna)**. The transfers reflect assets moving out of IPR&D as they progress to developed technology.

Pfizer says the 2025 impairments were primarily due to **changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts**. They included about **$1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin**, **$820 million for Tukysa (tucatinib)** and **$820 million for osivelotor**, among other IPR&D impairments. In total, the gross carrying amount rose by about **$2.9 billion**, from $18.9 billion to $21.8 billion. (2025 Form 10-K, Notes 4 and 10.)

Three filings identify the CODM as executives acting collectively:

- **JPMorgan Chase** — The **Operating Committee**, whose members act collectively as the Firm’s CODM. (2024 Form 10-K, p. 70)
- **Berkshire Hathaway** — The filing gives the group no name. It consists of the **Chairman and CEO, Vice Chairman of Insurance Operations, and Vice Chairman of Non-Insurance Operations**. (Note 26, p. K-108)
- **ExxonMobil** — The **Management Committee (MC)**, comprising the **CEO, CFO, and two Senior Vice Presidents** who oversee Upstream and Product Solutions as contact executives. (Note 18, p. 108)

The other five filings identify a single individual as CODM, rather than a group.

**Three of the eight filings** say a U.S. federal income tax audit was settled or resolved during fiscal 2024:

| Filing | Tax years covered |
|---|---|
| **NVIDIA** | **2018–2019** — the IRS audit was resolved in fiscal Q3 2024. (Form 10-K, p. 41) |
| **Pfizer** | **2016–2018** — the federal audit was effectively settled in fiscal Q3 2024. (Form 10-K, p. 74) |

- **Crude oil:** Prices eased from their 2022 highs as markets normalized. In the first half of 2023, higher inventory levels pushed prices down toward the pre-COVID 10-year range. The company also cited crude-price moderation as growing liquids supply met record demand.
- **Natural gas:** Prices fell significantly during the first nine months as storage rose above historical averages in the U.S. and Europe, reflecting higher supply and lower demand. Prices improved in the fourth quarter with higher U.S. heating demand and supply interruptions in Europe and Asia.
